standard_prerequisites.name: Equivalence of categories
standard_prerequisites.statement: F is an equivalence of categories when there is G with natural isomorphisms 1_A ~ GF and FG ~ 1_B.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the first of the two properties shown equivalent.

standard_prerequisites.name: Isomorphism of categories
standard_prerequisites.statement: F is an isomorphism of categories when it is fully faithful and its object map is an equivalence of types.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the second property, and the converse direction starts from it.

standard_prerequisites.name: Equivalence of precategories versus full faithfulness plus split essential surjectivity
standard_prerequisites.statement: For precategories these two notions agree.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the retained result invoked at the end of the converse direction.

core_obligations: Observe that both properties are mere propositions, so it suffices to prove a logical equivalence (source line 816).

Forward direction: from an equivalence with inverse G and natural isomorphisms eta, epsilon, use the retained functor-category result to obtain identities between the composites and the identities, hence identities between the object maps, so that the object map of F is an equivalence of types (source lines 817-820).

Converse: assume F is fully faithful with invertible object map and let G_0 be its inverse on objects; for each b the unit gives an isomorphism F G_0 b ~ b, so F is split essentially surjective on objects (source lines 822-823).
Apply the retained characterisation of equivalences of precategories to conclude that F is an equivalence of categories (source line 824).

proof_roadmap.step: Reduce to a logical equivalence of two mere properties.
Forward direction via identities of composites and of object maps.
Converse direction via split essential surjectivity and the retained characterisation.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is Lemma 9.4.14 at source lines 812-814: for categories A and B a functor is an equivalence of categories if and only if it is an isomorphism of categories. The author's proof (source lines 815-825) is short because both properties are mere propositions, but each direction consumes a different retained result: the forward direction turns the natural isomorphisms into identities of the composites with the retained functor-category theorem and then reads off that the object map is an equivalence (lines 817-820), while the converse builds split essential surjectivity from the inverse object map (lines 822-823) and invokes the retained characterisation of equivalences of precategories to finish (line 824). The statement is a two-way implication between named notions and records neither of the two inputs nor the reduction of the properties to propositions.
